table.title: Slow motion and fast forward: The effects of changing the speed of mental simulation
table.data_collection_started: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
A great deal of research in cognitive science has examined the effects of changing either the contents or spatial framing of the imagination, but hardly any work has examined the effects of changing the temporal reference frame of mental scenes. For an ideal mental simulation, changing the rate at which something is imagined should not matter for the properties of the scene (running a video in double-time or slow-motion does not change the content of the video). However, it is unknown whether and how varying the temporal rates of the imagination affects the contents of an imagined scene for people. The current study will examine whether and how asking people to imagine mental scenes happening in ‘slow motion’ or ‘sped up’ affects the properties and contents of the imagined scene.

In each trial, participants will view clips with different playback speeds of projectile motion (Study 1: animated scenes; Study 2: naturalistic scenes) or pendulum motion (Study 3). Participants will be asked to mentally simulate how events would continue to unfold, and to judge when and where certain events would take place. Our choice of stimuli will be set up in advance such that the judgement of when an event would happen tracks changes to reference frame speed, while where an event would happen tracks changes to content speed.

We will ask whether the mind can represent a distortion in reference frame speed independent of the content speed and adjust mental simulation accordingly, by examining whether participants think the object actually moves faster when the video is sped up and vice versa. We do not predict a specific finding ahead of time. We will specify 4 different models of mental simulation that predict different patterns of results for these two effects (when and where).
table.design_dependent_variables:
We will conduct three studies, each comprising two task conditions: a “when” task and a “where” task. We will recruit an independent group of participants for each task condition in each study, resulting in six independent groups.

The video stimuli will differ across studies. In Study 1, participants will view animations of a cart moving toward a cliff, which will pause just before the cart reaches the edge. In Study 2, participants will view videos of a person pushing a yoga ball toward the edge of a ledge, which will pause just before the ball reaches the edge. In Study 3, participants will view videos of a person pushing a backpack suspended from a rope, which will pause when the backpack reaches the lowest point of its swing.

In all studies, the videos will be played at different playback speeds, and participants will be asked to continue the video in their mind. Within each study, participants in the two task conditions will view the same video stimuli but provide different responses.

In the “when” task condition, participants will need to press the ‘J’ key on their keyboard when they think the cart/ball would first contact the ground (Studies 1 and 2) or the backpack would reach the opposite end of its arc. The dependent variable is the estimated falling/swinging time, measured as the duration (in seconds) between the end of the video and the keyboard press.

In the “where” task condition, participants will click on the screen to indicate where they think the cart or the ball would first contact the ground (Studies 1 and 2) or where the backpack would reach the opposite end of its swing (Study 3). In Studies 1 and 2, the dependent variable will be the estimated travel distance, measured as the horizontal distance between the click position and the bottom of the cliff or the ledge. In Study 3, the dependent variable will be the estimated swinging angle, measured as the angle between the vertically downward line through the rope’s pivot point and the line connecting the pivot point to the participant’s click location.
table.study_design_overview:
The three studies share a primary within-subject manipulation: 

Playback speed. The playback speed will have six levels: 0.5x, 0.75x, 1x, 1.25x, 1.5x, and 2x. The playback speed will be displayed at the top-left corner of the screen. Additional dynamic cues will convey the playback speed manipulations: a timer in the top-right corner will show the time passing in ``seconds : hundredths of a second" format; a red dot next to the timer will flash once per second. Both cues will speed up or slow down with playback.

Study 1 will include two additional within-subject manipulations. Both will be defined relative to a square canvas with an edge length of 1280 pixels:

1. Cliff height, with two levels: 384 or 895 pixels.

2. Cart speed, with three levels: 200, 250, or 300 pixels per second, defined at 1x playback speed.

Studies 2 and 3 will also include two additional within-subject manipulations:

1. Base video. We will include 6 different base videos showing the ball (Study 2) or backpack (Study 3) moving at different speeds. Each base video will then be presented at each of the six playback speeds specified above.

2. Video orientation. On each trial, the video will be randomly presented either in its original orientation or horizontally mirrored. Each participant will view each combination of base video and playback speed only once. The primary analysis will pool responses across video orientations after accounting for mirroring, coding travel distance (Studies 1 and 2) and swing angle (Study 3) as positive in the expected direction and negative in the opposite direction.

All three studies will also include a between-subject manipulation: 

Task condition. Participants will be assigned to one of two task conditions. In the “when” task condition, participants will press the “J” key when they think the cart or ball would first contact the ground (Studies 1 and 2) or the backpack would reach the opposite endpoint of its swing (Study 3). In the “where” task condition, participants will click on the screen to indicate the estimated landing position of the cart or ball (Studies 1 and 2) or the location of the opposite end of the backpack’s arc (Study 3).
table.statistical_tests:
**Mental Simulation Models**

We will implement four computational models that differ in terms of how they will take into account changes in reference speed and content speed. 

To illustrate the distinction, consider a video filming a cart moving towards a cliff at velocity v with a falling time of t and a travel distance d = v * t. The video is then played at double time with playback speed ps = 2, leading to the perceived cart velocity v’ = ps * v = 2v and a perceived falling time t’ = t / ps = t / 2. Note that, for a fixed cliff height, the falling time depends only on the playback speed but not the cart's velocity, whereas the landing distance only depends on the cart’s velocity but not the playback speed. Now consider four models: 

(1) Full Model: According to this model, people do notice and take into account the change in reference frame, and take into account the resulting change in content speed. This model will calculate an estimate of the change in playback speed est(ps) and use it to adjust the perceived velocity v’ to obtain content speed est(v) = v’ / est(ps) as well as the falling time est(t’) = t / est(ps). Such a model would successfully predict timing and distance judgements in the example above.

(2) Default Model: According to this model, people do not take into account the change in reference frame. Whatever events they observe are taken to be happening in real time. For this model, est(ps) = 1, and therefore, the estimated velocity of things in a scene are simply the observed velocity. Such a model would not correctly predict when or where events occur in our stimuli.

(3) Reference-Frame-Only Model: According to this model, people do notice and take into account changes in the playback speed like the Full, but do not apply the required change to the perceived speed. The model will correctly compute the falling time as est(t’) = t / est(ps), but incorrectly estimate the content velocity as est(v) = v’. Taken together, such a model would correctly predict changes to ground truth timing but not distance.

(4) Content-Only Model: According to this model, people do notice and adjust for changes in content speed, but they do not apply these changes to the reference frame. The model would correctly estimate the content velocity as est(v) = v’ / est(ps)  but incorrectly compute the falling time as est(t’) = t. Taken together, such a model would correctly predict changes to ground truth distance but not timing.

Additional note for Study 3:

We note that the known separation between pendulum period and angular speed is obtained by using approximations that assume small angle differences. In real life, the period increases slightly with the increase in pendulum's speed. However, this does not confound the analysis: If participants represent the content and reference frame speed separately, the period should decrease with the increase of the playback speed. If participants instead simulate the pendulum's motion using the directly perceived angular velocity, the simulated angular velocity of the pendulum would increase with the playback speed, and the period would increase with the increase in the playback speed. 

Model Adjustment:

Participants may systematically deviate from ground truth perception for either reference frame speed or content speed. A person could recognize a double-speed video is sped up but incorrectly represent its playback speed as ps = 1.8. Or, the person could incorrectly represent the cart as moving at 1.1v even when the video is played at 1x playback speed. Such mistakes in perception can lead to deviations from ground truth independently of our interest here. To account for these possible errors, we will adjust model outputs to be in line with human data in the following two ways: 

(i) We will assume that participants’ estimates of reference-frame speed are a linear function of ground-truth playback speed: est(playback speed) = ps_a * (ground truth playback speed) + ps_b. We will estimate ps_a and ps_b by fitting participants’ estimated playback speed as a linear function of ground truth playback speed. For each trial, the estimated playback speed will be computed as the falling/swinging time in 1x playback speed divided by participants’ estimated falling/swinging time. This adjustment will be applied to models’ playback speed estimation.

(ii) We will assume that participants’ estimates of content speed are a linear function of ground-truth content speed: est(content speed) = ct_a * (ground truth content speed) + ct_b. We will estimate the ct_a and ct_b by fitting participants’ estimated content speed as a linear function of ground truth content speed in trials with 1x playback speed. In Studies 1 and 2, est(content speed) = est(v) = est(travel distance) / t, where t is the ground truth falling time in 1x playback speed; in Study 3: est(content speed) = est(ω) = sqrt((2 * g / L) * (1 - cos(est(swinging angle)))), where L is the length of the rope and g is gravity. The adjustment will be applied to the models' content speed at each simulation step.

Both adjustment functions will be estimated and applied separately for each study. Within each study, the same adjustment functions will be used across models, so that any remaining difference between the model results will be due to the workings of the models themselves.

We will perform the analysis below separately on each study.

[“When” Task]


The falling/swinging time after playback speed manipulation (t') is inversely proportional to the playback speed (ps) such that t' = t / ps, where t is the falling/swinging time in 1x playback speed. Therefore, the variables will be log-transformed to express this multiplicative relationship as a linear one: log(t') = log(t) − log(ps). 

In Study 1, we will predict participants’ log(falling time estimate) with log(playback speed) and log(ground truth falling time at 1x playback speed) as fixed effects and participants as random effects. In Study 2, we will use the same linear mixed-effects model as in Study 1, except that we will omit log(ground truth falling time at 1x playback speed) as a predictor because it will be constant in Study 2. In Study 3, we will predict participants' log(swinging time estimate) with log(playback speed) and log(ground truth swinging time at 1x playback speed) as fixed effects and participants as random effects. We will then evaluate which model captures participants' representation of playback speed in the following ways:

1. Qualitative analysis: For the data simulated by each model: in Study 1, we will use a linear regression model predicting log(falling time estimate) with log(playback speed) and log(ground truth falling time at 1x playback speed); in Study 2, we will apply the same linear regression model but omit the regressor log(ground truth falling time at 1x playback speed); in Study 3, we will predict log(swinging time estimate) with log(playback speed) and log(ground truth swinging time at 1x playback speed). For the human data, we will use a linear mixed-effects model with the same fixed effects and participant-specific random intercepts. Models that reproduce the playback speed effect observed in human behavior, including the statistical significance and directions, will be considered to provide better qualitative accounts of human behavior.

2. Binary slope comparison: For the human data and the data simulated by each model, we will fit the linear model as specified in (1) and compute the slope of log(playback speed). We will calculate the 95% confidence intervals of the slopes with stats::confint function in R. We will evaluate the models with slope confidence intervals overlapping with humans' as the ones better predicting human behavior.

3. Model correlation tests: We will aggregate the human and model-generated time estimates into 36 condition-level means (Study 1: two height x three cart speed x six playback speeds; Studies 2 and 3: six base videos x six playback speeds). For each model, we will compute mean squared error (MSE) and Pearson's correlation coefficient (r). The confidence intervals for each of them will be obtained through participant-level bootstrapping. Models with lower MSE and higher Pearson's r will be considered to provide better fits to human behavior.

In contrast, a model that simulates the scene using its uncorrected perceived (angular) velocity, such as Default model or Reference-Frame-Only model, will carry the perceived (angular) velocity into the simulation, making the estimated travel distance or swinging angle associated with the playback speed.

In Study 1 and 2, estimate travel distance (d) might be computed as the product of falling time at 1x playback speed (t) and perceived velocity (v’): d = t * v’ = t * v * ps, where v is the horizontal velocity at 1x playback speed, and ps is the playback speed. To express the multiplicative relationship as a linear one, we will log-transform the variables: log(d) = log(v) + log(t) + log(ps). In Study 3, under the small angle approximation, the swinging angle (θ) might be estimated as the product of perceived angular velocity(ω) and a constant determined by the rope length (L) and gravity (g):  θ  ≈ ω’ * sqrt(L / g) = ω * ps * sqrt(L / g), where ω is the angular velocity at 1x playback speed, and ps is the playback speed. In Study 2, we will use the same linear mixed-effects model as in Study 1, except omitting log(falling time at 1x playback speed) as a predictor. In Study 3, we will predict participants' log(swinging angle estimate) with log(playback speed) and log(ground truth angular velocity at 1x playback speed) as fixed effects and participants as random effects. In Study 2, we will use the same regression model but omit the falling time at 1x playback speed as a predictor. 2. Binary slope comparison: For the human data and the data simulated by each model, we will fit the linear models as specified in (1) and obtain the coefficient for log(playback speed). table.outliers_and_exclusions:
We will use two pre-screening procedures to make sure participants understand the task correctly and to avoid data generated by AI-bots.

1. We have 4 multi-choice questions testing participants’ understanding of the task. Any participants answering at least one question incorrectly will be redirected to the beginning of the instruction, and only participants who complete all of the questions correctly can proceed to the experiment.

2. To avoid data generated by AI-bots, we will implement cognitive traps which humans can pass easily while AI-bots will fail systematically. The traps included in the experiments are “Checker Shadow” (Ullman, 2024) and “Moving Robot.” (Affonso, 2026) Any participants who fail any of the cognitive traps will not be able to proceed to the experiment and will be blocked for further participation.

Additionally, trials with invalid responses will be excluded from analysis. Invalid trials are defined as follows:

- “When” experiment: Responses are invalid if they occur before or at the moment the video pauses (estimated time to the target event <= 0).

- “Where” experiment: In Studies 1 and 2, responses are invalid if the estimated landing position is on the wrong side of or directly below the cliff or ledge edge (travel distance <= 0), or if the click is way above the ground (normalized y position < 0.8). In Study 3, responses are invalid if the click is on the wrong side of the swing or directly on the vertically downward line through the rope’s pivot point (swinging angle <= 0), or if the estimated rope length, the distance between the click position and the pivot of the pendulum, is too long or too short (rope length < 550 pixels or rope length > 1050 pixels). These exclusions will be applied after accounting for mirroring, with travel distance and swing angle coded as positive in the expected direction and negative in the opposite direction.

We will exclude any participant with four or more invalid trials.

Reference: 
Ullman, Tomer. "The illusion-illusion: Vision language models see illusions where there are none." arXiv preprint arXiv:2412.18613 (2024).
Affonso, Felipe M. (2026), “Brief Commentary: A Framework for Detecting AI Agents in Online Research,” Journal of Consumer Research. https://doi.org/10.1093/jcr/ucag006
table.sample_size: We will recruit 40 participants for each experiment before exclusion, for a total of 80 participants for each study and 240 subjects across the project.
table.additional_comments:
We will include the following analysis as secondary analyses:

1. We will perform the same analyses specified in Analyses Section on the unadjusted model. 

2. We will repeat these analyses without log-transforming the variables:

- "When" experiment: In Study 1 and 3, we will use a generalized mixed-effects model with Gamma distribution to correlate the estimated time with the inverse of the playback speed and the time in 1x playback speed as fixed effects, and participants as random intercepts. In Study 2, we will use the same generalized mixed-effects model but omit the the time in 1x playback speed as a predictor.

- "Where" experiment: In Study 1, we will use a mixed-effects model to predict participants’ travel distance estimate with playback speed, velocity at 1x playback speed, and falling time at 1x playback speed as fixed effects and participants as random effects. In Study 2, we will use the same linear mixed-effects model as in Study 1, except that we will omit falling time at 1x playback speed as a predictor. In Study 3, we will predict participants' swinging angle estimate with playback speed and angular velocity at 1x playback speed as fixed effects and participants as random effects.

For an ideal mental simulation, changing the rate at which something is imagined should not matter for the properties of the scene (running a video in double-time or slow-motion does not change the content of the video). However, it is unknown whether and how varying the temporal rates of the imagination affects the contents of an imagined scene for people. The current study will examine whether and how asking people to imagine mental scenes happening in ‘slow motion’ or ‘sped up’ affects the properties and contents of the imagined scene.

In each trial, participants will view clips with different playback speeds of projectile motion (Study 1: animated scenes; Study 2: naturalistic scenes) or pendulum motion (Study 3). Participants will be asked to mentally simulate how events would continue to unfold, and to judge when and where certain events would take place. Our choice of stimuli will be set up in advance such that the judgement of when an event would happen tracks changes to reference frame speed, while where an event would happen tracks changes to content speed.

We will ask whether the mind can represent a distortion in reference frame speed independent of the content speed and adjust mental simulation accordingly, by examining whether participants think the object actually moves faster when the video is sped up and vice versa. We do not predict a specific finding ahead of time. We will specify 4 different models of mental simulation that predict different patterns of results for these two effects (when and where).", "We will conduct three studies, each comprising two task conditions: a “when” task and a “where” task. In Study 2, participants will view videos of a person pushing a yoga ball toward the edge of a ledge, which will pause just before the ball reaches the edge. - “Where” experiment: In Studies 1 and 2, responses are invalid if the estimated landing position is on the wrong side of or directly below the cliff or ledge edge (travel distance <= 0), or if the click is way above the ground (normalized y position < 0.8). In Study 3, responses are invalid if the click is on the wrong side of the swing or directly on the vertically downward line through the rope’s pivot point (swinging angle <= 0), or if the estimated rope length, the distance between the click position and the pivot of the pendulum, is too long or too short (rope length < 550 pixels or rope length > 1050 pixels). These exclusions will be applied after accounting for mirroring, with travel distance and swing angle coded as positive in the expected direction and negative in the opposite direction.

We will exclude any participant with four or more invalid trials.

#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 1520 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (1520). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 384 columns across 28 data files.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 28 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Participants were asked to mentally simulate how events would continue to unfold, and judged when and where certain events would take place.
All studies were conducted online 34, recruiting US-based participants via Prolific (https://www.prolific.co.
Participants were compensated for their time at a rate of 12 USD per hour.
All participants provided informed consent.
In each experiment, we recruited 40 participants.
The animations stopped just as the cart reached the edge of the cliff, and participants were asked to imagine the continued motion of the cart.

In the "When" Experiment (Experiment 1a), participants were asked to continue the animation in their mind, and press a key at the moment when the cart would have hit the ground, had the animation continued.
We recruited 40 participants from Prolific for each experiment, and applied pre-registered exclusion criteria to them.

In the "When" Experiment, 3 participants were excluded for having 4 or more invalid trials; 2 participants failed to submit a complete dataset to our server; and 14 additional invalid trials were excluded, leaving 35 participants (21 female, 14 male; age: M = 44.8, SD = 12.1, range = 25-67) and 2506 trials for analysis.

In the "Where" Experiment, 2 participants were excluded for having 4 or more invalid trials; 1 participant failed to submit a complete dataset to our server; and 9 additional invalid trials were excluded, leaving 37 participants (20 female, 17 male; age: M = 41.1, SD = 12.2, range = 18-72) and 2655 trials for analysis.

The model showed a significant correlation between log estimated falling (i) Observe Participants were asked to continue the motion of the cart in their mind, and either answer when it hit the ground (Experiment 1a) or where it landed (Experiment 1b).
This can reflect that participants are not ideally sensitive to manipulations in the ground truth, and is accounted for in model adjustment (see earlier section).

Overall, our results suggest that participants are taking into account the distortion in reference frame rate when unfolding the adjusted scene in their mind, independent of the content speed, and both the Full and RF-Only models predict the timing judgement of participants.

This result suggests that participants are sensitive to the variation in carts' speed in the original video, such that the faster the cart moves, the further along the horizontal axis participants believe it will land.

Considering both experiments together: The results of our "When" experiment suggest that participants were generally sensitive to the manipulation of reference-frame speed, and adjusted their mental simulation to take place faster or slower as a whole.
However, instead of watching simplified animated stimuli, participants were shown videos of real scenes.
The video was clipped at the moment when the ball reached the edge of the ledge, and participants were asked to continue its motion in their mind (see Fig. 5).
We recruited 80 participants online via Prolific (40 for each experiment).
Each participant completed 350 36 trials.

In the "Where" Experiment, 3 participants were excluded for having 4 or more invalid trials, and 3 additional invalid trials were dropped, leaving 37 participants (26 female, 11 male); age: M = 50.3, SD = 13.4, range = 28-77) and 1329 trials analyzed.

A generalized linear mixed-effect model showed a significant negative correlation between the estimated log falling duration and the log playback speed (β = -0.76, SE = 0.020, t = -36.99, p < 0.0001), meaning participants were sensitive to the changes in frame-rate.
We first examined whether participants were sensitive to variation in the object speed in 1× videos.
Participants were asked to continue the motion of the bag in their mind, and either answer when it reached its apex (Experiment 3a, top), or where it reached its apex (Experiment 3b).
Participants were then asked to continue the bag's motion in their minds 3 .
In the "When" experiment (Experiment 3a), participants were asked to press a key at the moment they think the bag would reach the end of its arc, had it continued its motion.
In the "Where" experiment (Experiment 3b), a separate group of participants were asked to click on the screen, at the position that the bag would reach the apex of its arc, had the video continued.
We recruited 40 participants online via Prolific for each experiment.
Each participant completed 36 trials.

In the "When" Experiment, 2 participants were excluded for having 4 or more invalid trials; 1 participant failed to submit a complete data set to our server, and an additional 5 invalid trials were dropped 4 .

In the "Where" Experiment, 2 participants were excluded for having 4 or more invalid trials; 1 participant failed to submit a complete dataset to our server, and 12 additional invalid trials were dropped, leaving 37 participants (23 female, 13 male, 1 other or not reported; age: M = 44.2, SD = 11.7, range = 26-69) and 1320 trials for analysis. 3 We note that in pilot studies we first considered a scene in which one of the authors pushed another person in a local playground swing.

The repeating conclusion is that the data suggest that participants are indeed able to take into account the distortion in reference-frame rate when imagining how mental scenes unfold, independent of the content speed.
We first examined whether participants were sensitive to the variation in pendulum speed in 1× videos.
Participants were also given explicit instructions about the change in playback speed, and saw examples of 0.5×, 1×, and 2× clips at the start of the experiment.
Participants were asked to continue the motion of the cart in their mind, and either answer when it hit the ground (Experiment 1a) or where it landed (Experiment 1b).
Participants were shown a cart moving at different speeds, rolling off a cliff of different heights, in different playback speeds.
Participants were asked to continue the motion of the ball in their mind, and either answer when it hit the ground (Experiment 2a, top) or where it landed (Experiment 2b, bottom).

#### Execution
**The Python code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 13 scripts: 4 ran without error, 9 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 0 are written for Python 2 and not run. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions (e.g. in a `requirements.txt`). **A script looked for a file in another folder than the deposit has it**, so before running it once more we copied it there: `study1_animated_cart.zip/study1_animated_cart/experiment/when/assets/trial_info_new.json` to `study1_animated_cart.zip/study1_animated_cart/model/stimuli/trial_info_new.json` for `study1_animated_cart.zip/study1_animated_cart/model/build_scenes.py`. text.text: Research on the imagination has examined how changing the contents and spatial framing of a mental scenes changes that scene.
But hardly any work has changing the temporal reference frame of the imagination.
For an ideal simulator, changing the frame-rate in which something is imagined should not matter for scene content, but it is unknown whether changing the temporal frame affects people's imagination.

Across three studies and six experiments (N = 223 after exclusions), participants watched stylized and naturalistic scenarios of projectile and pendulum motion at different playback speeds, and continued them in their mind.
Our set-up dissociates temporal reference frame from content speed, which allowed us to compare people's predictions to simulation models that do or don't separate content from temporal frame.
We found that participants could adjust their imagined temporal reference.
Participants also kept content separate from reference-frame speed in realistic (but not stylized) scenes.
Suppose you're watching a game of soccer on television.
You see a ball kicked full force towards the goal, the goalie diving just in time to make the save.
The dramatic moment is then replayed in slow motion.
The goal-keeper now seems to float like an unhurried blimp towards the ball, as it drifts slowly to the goal.
Despite the change in visible motion, you're under no illusion that gravity has changed, or that the ball will hit the goalie with any less force.
But now consider: when you imagine something happening in slow-motion (like a ball moving slowly towards a face), do you actually disentangle the internal and external dynamics of the imagined this?
Does a ball moving in slow-motion in the mind move less far?
Any mental scene is made up of content (objects, characters, events, properties, and so on) and reference frames (spatial and temporal).
These two components, content and reference frame, can vary independently.
To go back to our opening example, you might imagine different players taking different shots in a soccer game.
This would be a change of the contents of your mental scene.
You could also imagine the exact same An example of an everyday scene unfolding at normal playback speed (1×).
One could either change the content speed, e.g. making the player and ball genuinely move faster, so that the ball travels farther in the same scene time.

Or, one could change the reference-frame speed, e.g. making the whole scene play at 2×, so events occur sooner relative to an external clock, but object velocities are unchanged. (b) The paradigm we used in our studies dissociate content properties and reference frame by using motion types that map changes in either content or reference frame to different judgements.
Here, we show the example of projectile motion, specifically a cart rolling off a cliff.
Increasing the horizontal cart speed will make it fall further, but not change its vertical speed, and so not change the time to impact.
Making the entire scene run faster will make the cart hit the ground sooner (relative to an external clock), but not change where it ends up.
So, having participants judge 'where' the cart ended up and 'when' it hit the ground allows us to work backwards to how they reason when speeding up or slowing down a mental scene.

This would be a change of spatial reference frame or perspective.
Importantly for us here, you could also vary the temporal reference frame of your imagination (see Fig. 24 1a).

text.text: That is, you could imagine a player truly moving more slowly or quickly towards the ball (a change in 25 content speed), or you could imagine the entire scene is unfolding more slowly or more quickly (a change While extensive previous research has examined how changes in spatial reference affect the imagination, hardly any work has examined whether and how changes in temporal reference affect the contents of the imagination.
Here, we asked: can the mind represent a change in reference-frame speed independent of a change in content speed?
That is: does speeding up or slowing down a mental simulation affect the contents of the mental simulation itself?

To address this question, we adopt an approach based on the notion that the mind can reason about the dynamics of everyday objects by running a kind of simplified, internal world model [1] [2] [3] [4] .
text.formatted: To address this question, we adopt an approach based on the notion that the mind can reason about the dynamics of everyday objects by running a kind of simplified, internal world model <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> .

text.text: On this approach, the mind runs a mental simulation that is akin to the simulations developed by engineers to capture simplified versions of the real world that run in approximately real time (for either scientific or entertainment purposes).
This approach has support from computational, behavioral, and neurological studies 5 , but it also has its alternatives and critiques [6] [7] [8] [9] .
text.formatted: This approach has support from computational, behavioral, and neurological studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> , but it also has its alternatives and critiques <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> .

text.text: Overall there appears to be a growing consensus that the mind is likely using different computations (or combining them) to solve different aspects of intuitive physics [10] [11] [12] , and that even if the mind does use mental simulation, then simulation must use a variety of principled approximations and workarounds 3, 13, 14.
text.formatted: Overall there appears to be a growing consensus that the mind is likely using different computations (or combining them) to solve different aspects of intuitive physics <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> , and that even if the mind does use mental simulation, then simulation must use a variety of principled approximations and workarounds <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref>.

text.text: Two main possibilities seem a priori possible: On one hand, the mind's mental simulation might work like an actual simulation, in which case speeding up or slowing down the reference-frame speed should not affect the content.
Hitting 'fast forward' on a video might make a player seem to move faster, but the ball they kick will not travel any further.
Events also appear faster relative to an external clock, not an internal one.
On the other hand, it is possible that the mind cannot disentangle inner and external clocks.

This may be because the mind does not start by establishing certain properties of the scene prior to generating a mental image, but rather 'reads off' those properties from the scene, including properties such as force and velocity, which in turn affect the next predicted image.
This may also come about because of resource limitations: pushing a computer game to run faster requires greater resources and so may result in loss of fidelity for aspects of the scene.

Beyond these two options, it is also possible for behavior to be mixed and nuanced, such that people will be better at separating reference-frame speed and content speed in some scenes, and not others.

The different options are not something that is immediately distinguished by introspection: we encourage the reader to try for themselves to imagine a person throwing a ball in double-time, and try to assess where the ball will end up or how hard it will hit a wall.
Previous research has examined related, but separate questions.
The separation between imagined content and reference frame has been extensively examined in spatial reference frames.

There is a vast literature on this topic, but for our purposes it is sufficient to note that a great deal of research has studied questions related to changing spatial frames in the imagination, including the use of allocentric vs. egocentric reference frames in memory, navigation, and imagination 15 , the adoption of different points of view on the same scene 16, 17 , the different functions and levels of abstraction associated with different spatial perspectives 18, 19 , the cognitive neuroscience parallels of different mental perspectives on a scene 20 , the development of perspective taking 21, 22 , and so on.
text.formatted: There is a vast literature on this topic, but for our purposes it is sufficient to note that a great deal of research has studied questions related to changing spatial frames in the imagination, including the use of allocentric vs. egocentric reference frames in memory, navigation, and imagination <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> , the adoption of different points of view on the same scene <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> , the different functions and levels of abstraction associated with different spatial perspectives <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref> , the cognitive neuroscience parallels of different mental perspectives on a scene <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref> , the development of perspective taking <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22</ref> , and so on.

text.text: At the risk of over-simplification, this research has generally found that changes to spatial reference can induce changes to the contents of mental simulation and their processing, and that different spatial references are associated with different functions, neural implementations, and developmental timelines.
By comparison to this line of work, much less work has examined the effect of changes in temporal reference frames on the imagination.
Beyond spatial frames, past work on the imagination has also studied the internal timing over which events unfold.

Experiments on mental transformations (such as rotation or translation) and mental scanning have found striking correspondence between the time that it would take to carry out such operations in reality, and the time that it takes to imagine them [23] [24] [25] [26] .
text.formatted: Experiments on mental transformations (such as rotation or translation) and mental scanning have found striking correspondence between the time that it would take to carry out such operations in reality, and the time that it takes to imagine them <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref> .

text.text: While this research has examined the speed of mental simulation, it did not examine the effects of asking participants to imagine scenes as happening in a faster or slower frame.

Research on the mental simulation of actions, movement, and motor imagery has also found a correspondence between the external timing and complexity of a given motion, and the time it takes to imagine this motion 27, 28 .
text.formatted: Research on the mental simulation of actions, movement, and motor imagery has also found a correspondence between the external timing and complexity of a given motion, and the time it takes to imagine this motion <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28</ref> .

text.text: This line of research sometimes asks people to imagine the action happening faster or slower 29 , but that question does not separate content speed (the action actually happening faster or slower) from reference-frame speed (the scene as a whole unfolding in slow motion or fast-forward).
text.formatted: This line of research sometimes asks people to imagine the action happening faster or slower <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29</ref> , but that question does not separate content speed (the action actually happening faster or slower) from reference-frame speed (the scene as a whole unfolding in slow motion or fast-forward).

text.text: Another related-but-separate area of research is the phenomenon of mental replay.

Previous work that studied human and non-human navigation, episodic memory, and the imagination of past and future events has found that replay of structured events happens in a compressed format [30] [31] [32] .
text.formatted: Previous work that studied human and non-human navigation, episodic memory, and the imagination of past and future events has found that replay of structured events happens in a compressed format <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref> .

text.text: That is, when people or nonhuman animals recall past episodes or paths (or run them forward), it appears that these events happen on a compressed timescale relative to their real-world counterparts.
Some early research took this compressed timescale to suggest that the (re)imagined events are played in an accelerated frame, like watching a video in fast-forward.

More recent research suggests that the compression is due to the replay's focus on the important moments of interest, more akin to watching snapshots or highlights of an event, which takes less time than watching the entire event again 33 .
text.formatted: More recent research suggests that the compression is due to the replay's focus on the important moments of interest, more akin to watching snapshots or highlights of an event, which takes less time than watching the entire event again <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33</ref> .

text.text: We do not mean to take up the question of what compression in replay represents, and only note that whatever the case, these studies do not focus on whether a directed change in mental frame rate affects the contents of the imagined scene.
Here, we examined whether the mind can represent a distortion in reference-frame speed independent of the content speed, and adjust mental simulation accordingly.

Across three studies and six experiments, participants viewed clips with different playback speeds of projectile motion (Study 1: animated scenes; Study 2: naturalistic scenes) or pendulum motion (Study 3).
Participants were asked to mentally simulate how events would continue to unfold, and judged when and where certain events would take place.
Our choice of stimuli was set up in advance such that the judgement of when an event happened tracked changes to reference-frame speed, while where an event happened tracked changes to content speed.
As we explain further in the methods, this mapping is not some universal feature of changes to mental simulation, but rather a generalizable and useful experimental design choice.

This separation also allows us to construct different mental simulation models that either do or do not take into account changes in reference frame, and then do or do not correctly use those to mentally simulate the contents of a scene.
To briefly summarize our results up front, we found that across all three studies the judgements of event timing varied with the playback speed.
This is expected, but important to establish, and it suggests that people do indeed take into account frame rate changes in their mental simulation.
In other words, a video shown in slow motion (or sped up) will be imagined as continuing in slow motion (or sped up).
Beyond this, we found that in animated scenes (Study 1), position judgements also varied with the playback speed, which suggests that in these scenes the content is affected by reference changes.
However, in the realistic scenes (Study 2 and 3), position judgements align with a model that distinctly represents frame-rate and content speed.

Taken altogether, our results suggest that (i) the mind can unfold scenes in sped-up or slowed-down frames, and (ii) this change in reference frame can have an effect on less familiar, stylized situations, but (iii) for realistic situations the mind is closer to an accurate simulation that does not actually change the properties of objects with the frame rate.

After detailing our results and models, we consider the possible reasons for, and implications of our findings, as well as future directions for the study of different temporal frames in the imagination.

text.text: Data for the main studies was collected on October 6, 2026.
In each experiment, we recruited 40 participants.

Sample sizes were determined on the basis of pilot studies, which were then used for a bootstrap analysis, indicating that 40 participants per experiment provide greater than 95% power to distinguish the hypotheses.
Across the experiments, we compared four possible mental simulation models, that differed in terms of how they took into account changes in reference-frame speed and content speed.
It is easiest to understand the differences between these models with reference to a simple example (see also Fig. 1b), which also parallels the stimuli for Studies 1 and 2.
text.formatted: It is easiest to understand the differences between these models with reference to a simple example (see also Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1b</ref>), which also parallels the stimuli for Studies 1 and 2.

text.text: Consider a toy cart moving horizontally from left to right along a table that is h = 1 meter in height.
The cart moves at a horizontal speed of v = 10 meters/second.
When the cart reaches the end of the table, it falls off.
Using basic Newtonian physics we know the time till the cart hits the ground is t = √︂ 2h g , and the horizontal distance that the cart will cover after it goes over the edge of the table is d = v•t.
Approximating g = 9.8 m s 2 , we get that the cart will take 0.45 seconds to hit the ground, and it will hit the ground 4.5 meters to the right of the edge of the table.
Next, suppose that all of this was initially filmed at a standard frame rate f .
This frame-rate could correspond to, say, 24 frames a second.
To make the following discussion and expressions easier, we can arbitrarily take the standard frame rate to be f = 1.

And lastly, suppose that the original video is now instead shown playing at double time, f ′ = 2 • f (this is why we set f = 1, so all that matters is the ratio between the new frame rate and the standard one).
So, the perceived speed of the cart will appear to an outside viewer to be v ′ = v • f ′ = 20 meter/second.
In terms of the outside clock, that is of the person watching the video, the cart will now hit the ground after t/ f ′ = 0.225 seconds.
This makes sense: the video is running twice as fast, the event of interest will happen in half the time.
But, what of the horizontal distance the cart will travel after rolling off the table ?
The speeding up of the video does not matter to this, as the cart is not actually traveling faster, and it will still cover a distance of d = v•t = 4.5 meters.

Notice that this scenario creates a clean mapping between 'when' judgements (time to fall) and expected changes in frame-rate, while 'where' judgements should not be affected by changes in frame rate.
This clean separation is not a generally true feature for randomly selected dynamic stimuli judgements, and is the reason we chose the stimuli we did.

With the motivating example of the cart in mind, what would a mental simulation account predict will happen, as people are asked to continue the motion of the cart past the edge of the table, in their imagination?

We considered four distinct models (see Fig. 2): (1) Full: According to this model, people do notice and take into account the change in reference frame, and also take into account the resulting change in content speed.
text.formatted: We considered four distinct models (see Fig. <ref type="figure">2</ref>): (1) Full: According to this model, people do notice and take into account the change in reference frame, and also take into account the resulting change in content speed.

text.text: This model calculates an estimation of the change in frame rate f ′ , and uses it to adjust the perceived velocity v ′ , and the timing of events t/ f ′ .
Such a model could successfully predict timing and distance judgements in the example above.
(2) Null: According to this model, people do not take into account the change in reference frame.
Whatever events they observe are taken to be happening in real time.
For this model, f ′ = f = 1, and therefore the estimated velocity of things in a scene is simply the observed velocity.
Such a model would not correctly predict when or where events occur in our stimuli.

(3) Reference-Frame-Only: According to this model, people do notice and take into account changes in the reference-frame speed like the Full model, but do not apply the required change to the perceived velocity.

To put this in plain terms, such a model is equivalent to a person perceiving (or imagining) a sped-up video and recognizing that the video is sped up, correctly anticipating some events will happen earlier as a result (for an external clock), but not then going the extra mental step of realizing that if the video is sped up, the content velocity must be slower than what they are seeing or imagining.
In our running example of the toy cart, such a model could correctly predict changes to ground truth timing, but not distance.
(4) Content-Speed-Only: According to this model, people do notice and adjust for changes in content speed, but they do not or cannot apply these likely a priori.

It would be equivalent to a person who recognizes a toy-cart video is sped up, correctly infers 172 the cart must be moving slower in terms of its original clock, but fails to recognize that events should be 173 taking place faster relative to an external clock, treating f ′ = f = 1 like the Null model.
Such a model could 174 correctly predict changes to ground truth distance but not timing, in our running example.

Consider seeing a cart rolling to the edge of a table and being asked to continue its motion in the imagination, when the scene is playing at different frame rates.

The Full model suggests people take into account that the entire scene is being sped up or slowed down, and correct for this in judging when the cart will hit the ground relative to an external clock, adjusting the perceived velocity accordingly.

The Reference-Frame-Only model suggests people take into account that the entire scene is being sped up or slowed down and so have accurate timing judgements, but do not correct the perceived velocity, such that frame-rate changes will influence final position.
The Content-Speed-Only model suggests people correct the perceived velocity, but do not adjust their timing judgements.
The Null model suggests people mentally continue the scene without any correction, taking e.g. a sped-up video to indicate a regular video in which the cart is simply moving faster.

Or, consider a person who watches a video playing at a standard frame rate, in which a cart moves at a speed of 3 m/s, but the person incorrectly perceives the cart as moving at 3.1 m/s.
Such errors in perception can lead to deviations from ground truth in a way that is not of interest to our current research.

To account for these possible errors, we adjusted model outputs to be in line with human data, in the following two ways: (i) Reference-frame speed was adjusted according to the empirical relationship between playback speed and participant timing judgements.

In other words, we use participants' own sensitivity to playback speed in 'when' judgements to allow for human misperception of frame-rate, such as a person that sees a video playing in double-time inaccurately thinking the adjusted frame-rate is 1.8 instead of 2.0; (ii) Content speed was adjusted according to the relationship between ground-truth content speed and participants' position estimation in the baseline conditions showing stimuli happening at regular frame rate (1×).
We emphasize this content-speed adjustment was estimated only from 1× trials, and then applied to non-1× trials.
This adjustment accounts for the potential perceptual errors, such as a person observing an object that is truly moving at 3 m/s, but perceiving it as moving at 3.1 m/s.

These two empirical adjustments were fixed by the data and applied equally to all models, so that any remaining difference between the model results would be due to the workings of the models themselves.
To summarize, we devised four distinct mental simulation models, which align with four different proposals for how people might imagine an entire mental scene as happening faster or slower.
These models make different predictions for how and when people deviate from ground truth judgements of when and where events take place.
The Full model suggests people can speed up or slow down their mental simulations, and adjust the content of simulations accordingly.
The Null model suggests that people cannot speed up or slow things down in the imagination, and that the frame rate for the imagined scene is treated as equal to the external clock.
The Reference-Frame-Only model suggests that people can adjust the timing of a mental simulation, but do not adjust the content correctly as a result.
The Content-Speed-Only model suggests that people can adjust the content of a mental simulation to account for sped-up or slowed-down scenes, but they do not adjust the frame-rate of the simulation.
We first examined how people continue the motion of a simple entity in their mind's eye, when the scene is presented as taking place either in standard time, or slowed down, or sped up.
Study 1 consisted of two different experiments.
In both experiments, participants viewed simple animations of a two-dimensional cart, moving horizontally towards the edge of a cliff (see Fig. 3).
text.formatted: In both experiments, participants viewed simple animations of a two-dimensional cart, moving horizontally towards the edge of a cliff (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>).

text.text: The animations stopped just as the cart reached the edge of the cliff, and participants were asked to imagine the continued motion of the cart.
Each animation was presented within a square canvas of 1280 × 1280 pixels.
We independently manipulated the cart's content speed (200, 250, or 300 pixels per second), the height of the cliff (384 or 895 pixels), and six playback speeds (0.5×, 0.75×, 1×, 1.25×, 1.5×, 2×).

We conveyed the playback speed of each animation in several ways, including both explicit-fixed cues and perceptual-dynamic cues: the rate itself was displayed at the top-left corner of the scene; a timer in the top-right corner showed the "internal The participants in both experiments described in this section saw the same animations of a cart rolling towards the edge of a cliff, and were all asked to continue the animations in their mind.
However, participants in the two experiments were given different instructions of how to react.

In the "When" Experiment (Experiment 1a), participants were asked to continue the animation in their mind, and press a key at the moment when the cart would have hit the ground, had the animation continued.
The duration between the animation freezing and a participant key press was logged as the estimated falling duration.
In the "Where"

Experiment (Experiment 1b), a different group of participants was asked to continue the animation in their mind and click on the screen, at the location where the cart would have landed, had the animation continued.
The horizontal distance between a participant's click and the bottom of the cliff was logged as the estimated travel distance.

As explained earlier, we chose projectile motion because it provides a natural dissociation between reference-frame speed and content speed: Given the same cliff height, changing the speed of the cart as it moves horizontally along the plateau changes where the cart will land after it flies off the cliff, but not when it lands.
Conversely, changing the playback speed of the video itself changes the landing time (relative to an external clock), but not the location of where the cart ends up.

Therefore, participants' estimated timing judgement provides a measure of participants' represented reference-frame speed, and their estimation of the landing position of the cart is a measure of their content speed representation.
We recruited 40 participants from Prolific for each experiment, and applied pre-registered exclusion criteria to them.

In the "When" Experiment, 3 participants were excluded for having 4 or more invalid trials; 2 participants failed to submit a complete dataset to our server; and 14 additional invalid trials were excluded, leaving 35 participants (21 female, 14 male; age: M = 44.8, SD = 12.1, range = 25-67) and 2506 trials for analysis.

In the "Where" Experiment, 2 participants were excluded for having 4 or more invalid trials; 1 participant failed to submit a complete dataset to our server; and 9 additional invalid trials were excluded, leaving 37 participants (20 female, 17 male; age: M = 41.1, SD = 12.2, range = 18-72) and 2655 trials for analysis.
We applied our pre-registered analysis plan to both experiments in this section.

As a mid-point summary, the "where" experiment shows that participants' judgments of content properties were affected by frame-rate changes.
The specific performance does not fall within any of the models, but is closer to the Reference-frame-only or Null models.
It suggests that the mind can discount some, but not all of the changes to the frame-rate of the mental scene when recovering the content speed.

Considering both experiments together: The results of our "When" experiment suggest that participants were generally sensitive to the manipulation of reference-frame speed, and adjusted their mental simulation to take place faster or slower as a whole.
This speaks against the Null and Content-Speed-Only models.

Our "Where" experiment findings show that participants can partially adjust the properties of mental simulation following the change in temporal reference frame, but not fully, with their performance falling between the Reference-Frame-Only and Full model.

In other words: When speeding up the mental scene, participants seemed to imagine the objects inside the scene as actually moving faster, though to a lesser extent than the direct increase in perceived motion.
Our use of simple animated scenes was an intentional choice, meant to help isolate extraneous factors and features.
But, it leaves open the possibility that people change content properties differently when given realistic motion cues.
To examine this, we conducted additional experiments that kept the logic of Study 1, but used realistic scenes.

While we varied our experiments so far in terms of content speed, temporal frame-rate, participant response, and realism of the scenes, they all focused on one kind of motion (projectile motion following horizontal launching).
To better establish the generality of the findings to other types of realistic motion, we next moved from projectile to pendulum motion.
4 Study 3: "When" and "Where" Task with realistic pendulums Study 1 and 2 considered how people represent and simulate projectile motion across changes to the temporal reference frame.
We used stimuli that depicted projectile motion (following horizontal launching) because it cleanly mapped different parts of motion to changes in content or reference-frame speeds.
We next examined people's behavior when presented with a different kind of stimuli, which showed pendulum motion.

We chose this type of stimuli as it also dissociates between reference-frame and content speed: Given the same rope length, changing a pendulum's angular velocity (scene content) will change where the pendulum reaches its highest point, but not the pendulum's period; changing the frame-rate of the scene as a whole (temporal reference frame) will change only the pendulum's period, not where it ends up at its apex.
We note that the known separation between pendulum period and angular speed is obtained by using approximations that assume small angle differences.
In real life, the period increases slightly with the increase in the pendulum's speed.

However, this does not confound our analysis here: If participants represent the content and reference-frame speed separately, then the period should decrease when the entire scene is sped increase with the increase in the playback speed.

Taken together with the results of Experiment 3a, the analysis suggests that participants (i) do understand a sped-up or slowed-down video is different in terms of its temporal reference frame, (ii) use the altered reference frame when imagining what takes place next, and (iii) can adjust the content of an imagined scene accordingly.
As with Study 2, the results of Study 3 suggest that people's apparent incorrect adjustment to content speed in simplified stimuli (Study 1) was due to a lack of realistic/familiar motion cues.
A mental scene has its contents: imagining a porcelain cup sliding along on a slippery table towards a slab of concrete is not the same as imagining a garbage truck sliding on ice.
The contents of a mental scene have their properties, and those have consequences: imagining a cup sliding after a gentle push will end differently than imagining that cup traveling at great speed.
This is all quite obvious so far.
But, a mental scene also has its reference frames: do you see the cup sliding from the point of view of the person who pushed it, or from the point of view of the cup?
Much of the research on mental simulation has studied the content of imagined scenes, and nearly all the work on reference frames has studied changes in spatial frames and perspective.
Here, we examined a different basic component of reference in the imaginationthe rate at which a mental scene moves.
In principle, the content of a mental scene is independent of its reference frames.
Speeding up a video of a porcelain cup hitting concrete will not make the shards fly any farther.
But for the human mind, content and the temporal reference frame may be linked.
Imagining the entire scene of the unfortunate porcelain cup speeding up might indeed make the shards fly farther in the mind.
Here, we asked: does the mind represent changes in the temporal reference frame independent of the content of imagined scenes, and does it adjust mental simulations accordingly?
We investigated how people imagine the simple motion of objects, when asked to speed up or slow down the imagined scene as a whole.

Specifically, we showed people projectile motion and pendulum motion at different frame rates, and then asked them to continue the events in their mind's eye, and judge when and where certain events took place.
The use of this type of motion lets us dissociate reference-frame speed and content speed, by mapping them separately onto judgements of timing and position.
We used stylized animations, and realistic videos.
Across three studies and six experiments, we found that: (i) People were generally able to adjust the playback speed of their mental simulation for all scenes.
Carts and balls in slow motion fell slower to the ground in the mind's eye, pendulums in half-time swung slower. (ii) People could recover and adjust imagined content separately from reference frame.
However, for stylized animations, people did not adjust the content fully.
People's results for stylized animations were best explained by a
Reference-Frame-Only mental simulation model, and their results for realistic scenes were best explained by a Full mental simulation model.
The results and models suggest that people can in principle separate imagined content and temporal reference frame, but this separation did not happen fully for stylized animations.

When considered from the perspective of a limited mental game engine account 2,3 , the following might be taking place: In order to unfold an imagined scene step by step, a mental simulation needs to fix the initial properties of entities (including their velocity V ), and the frame-rate of the simulation as a whole, F. In our experiments, both V and F were informed by perception.
On this view, perception is handing off to simulation the input that the frame-rate appears to be f ′ , and the velocity appears to be v.
But it is a separate mental operation to then adjust v to account for f ′ .
Realistic motion cues may directly affect the apparent v that is being handed off.
Our current studies open up many directions for future exploration in studying the effects of temporal rate distortion on the contents of mental simulation and the imagination.
We next consider a few of the important ones.
First, while we studied how speeding up or slowing down mental simulation might distort the speed of objects in the imagination, other properties may change in different ways.
More particularly, the read-out of mental-simulation may be distorted in different ways than the input that controls its next step.

To put this distinction in terms of a mental game engine framework: properties that determine the initial setup of the mental simulation (or propel it forward via a step-by-step transition function) may be differently affected by frame-rate changes than the modules that take the image-based output of mental simulation as their input, and such downstream modules are likely shared by both perception and imagination.
To give some examples of how these may play out differently: try to imagine an open palm moving at great speed but in slow motion directly towards a face.
You may see the moment of contact of the palm with the face, the ripples on the cheeks of the person being hit, and their slow and anguished turning away from the palm.
You may correctly judge that such a strike is painful, but even so you may lack the implicit perception of the striking force that accompanies such a scene playing in real time.
Compare this also to imagining a hand striking a face in double time.
Such a slap might 'feel' even more forceful than it is if seen in real time.
Moving beyond simple physical properties, higher-level inferences that are downstream of imagined scenes may be affected by mental speed-up and slow-down.

In direct perception, sped-up and slowed-down videos are known to affect higher-level judgements, from aesthetics 35 and intentionality 36, 37 , to luxury 38 , which suggests that imagined scenes may be affected in similar ways.
text.formatted: In direct perception, sped-up and slowed-down videos are known to affect higher-level judgements, from aesthetics <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">35</ref> and intentionality <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">36,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">37</ref> , to luxury <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">38</ref> , which suggests that imagined scenes may be affected in similar ways.

text.text: Beyond testing the distortion of additional properties, another direction to explore would be temporal distortions that are entirely self-generated, as opposed to a continuation of perceptual scenes.
In our studies, we had participants view videos and then asked them to continue those events in their mind's eye.
However, people can also imagine things happening in a slowed down or sped up way without direct perceptual input (we asked the reader to do so throughout this paper).
This route would bypass the direct input of perception, and may lead to different content adjustments.

However, we caution that while it is easy enough simply to ask people to imagine things happening faster or slower, it is experimentally difficult to determine how people then continue things in the imagination given such instructions.

While previous studies on mental transformations (such as scanning or rotation) could rely on a standard and consistent notion of an internal clock to draw conclusions about the speed of mental simulation, in our suggested manipulations both content and frame-rate can vary and are coupled.
This makes it challenging for the experimenter to separately determine both of these changes, without starting from some agreed on perceptual input (as in our stimuli).
We have not resolved this issue ourselves, and leave it as a challenge for further research.
A third important direction for future research would examine the degree to which speeding up and slowing down an entire imagined scene takes a toll on mental resources.
While an ideal, limitless simulation can run things at whatever frame-rate desired, in practice changes to frame-rate come with a cost.

To the degree that filling in the details of a specific moment in an imagined scene takes time, moving faster between frames will reduce the level of details available at each frame, predicting a loss of imagery-related detail (though the distinction between physical-spatial reasoning and graphical rendering 39 may affect loss of spatial vs. graphical detail differently).
text.formatted: To the degree that filling in the details of a specific moment in an imagined scene takes time, moving faster between frames will reduce the level of details available at each frame, predicting a loss of imagery-related detail (though the distinction between physical-spatial reasoning and graphical rendering <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">39</ref> may affect loss of spatial vs. graphical detail differently).

text.text: Conversely, imagining things in slow-motion may allow for greater filling in of detail, but tax memory resources as a result.
The ability to speed up and slow down animations and videos is a recent invention in human history.
In asking the reader to imagine things as happening faster or slower, we have relied on the implicit assumption that they are familiar with relevant examples from daily life.
Our experiments were with adult participants based in the US, and similarly have an implicit assumption of familiarity of sped-up and slowed-down events.
The fact that participants could generally adjust for temporal frame-rate and content properties suggests they understood the manipulation and backs up this implicit assumption.
But, it is possible that notions of speeding up or slowing down scenes in the imagination make no sense to someone unfamiliar with relevant technology.
We accept this as a limitation of the current research, and cross-cultural and developmental studies are necessary to establish the generality of the findings.

But, we would also note that for spatial reference, surveys on memory that predate film and television found that people spontaneously recall or imagine a scene from a third-person perspective 40 , despite having no experience with being outside of their bodies, or observing the relevant technique in films.
text.formatted: But, we would also note that for spatial reference, surveys on memory that predate film and television found that people spontaneously recall or imagine a scene from a third-person perspective <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">40</ref> , despite having no experience with being outside of their bodies, or observing the relevant technique in films.

text.text: This suggests that at least in principle, some reference changes in the imagination are possible without direct experience of the changes.

In addition, old tales of whole lifetimes unfolding in the imagination while mere moments pass in real life (such as Shen Jiji's "The World Inside a Pillow") and pre-modern academic discussions of internal time as separate from external time 41 also suggestively point to a basic cognitive distinction between internal and external timing (though we emphasize they do not directly line up with the notion of the imagined things themselves being represented as taking place faster or slower to the mental observer).
text.formatted: In addition, old tales of whole lifetimes unfolding in the imagination while mere moments pass in real life (such as Shen Jiji's "The World Inside a Pillow") and pre-modern academic discussions of internal time as separate from external time <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41</ref> also suggestively point to a basic cognitive distinction between internal and external timing (though we emphasize they do not directly line up with the notion of the imagined things themselves being represented as taking place faster or slower to the mental observer).

text.text: Again, further cross-cultural work and developmental work is needed to examine and establish the generality of the findings.
The imagination can feel like it is conjuring up a play inside our heads.
But we must distinguish the stage directions from the set and players.
People may call to mind different players, and have them read different lines, or move the audience to different perspectives.
Here, we explored a different kind of direction: running the whole scene fast or slow.
We found that for realistic scenes, people can do this, while keeping a separation between the tempo and the players.
For stylized scenes, the change in imagined time bled into the imagined scenes.
But whatever the pace, eventually it's curtains.

Figure1.
Changing the content or reference frame of scenes. (a) An example of an everyday scene unfolding at normal playback speed (1×).
One could either change the content speed, e.g. making the player and ball genuinely move faster, so that the ball travels farther in the same scene time.

Or, one could change the reference-frame speed, e.g. making the whole scene play at 2×, so events occur sooner relative to an external clock, but object velocities are unchanged. (b) The paradigm we used in our studies dissociate content properties and reference frame by using motion types that map changes in either content or reference frame to different judgements.
Here, we show the example of projectile motion, specifically a cart rolling off a cliff.
Increasing the horizontal cart speed will make it fall further, but not change its vertical speed, and so not change the time to impact.
Making the entire scene run faster will make the cart hit the ground sooner (relative to an external clock), but not change where it ends up.
So, having participants judge 'where' the cart ended up and 'when' it hit the ground allows us to work backwards to how they reason when speeding up or slowing down a mental scene.

Figure 3.
Study 1.
Participants viewed a simple animation of a cart rolling off the edge of a cliff at different heights, horizontal velocities, and playback speeds.
Participants were asked to continue the motion of the cart in their mind, and either answer when it hit the ground (Experiment 1a) or where it landed (Experiment 1b).

Participants in the "when" experiment showed a sensitivity to changes in playback speed (the faster the playback, the sooner they thought the cart will hit the ground), generally in line with models that adjust for frame-rate in mental simulation, and not in line with those that do not.
However, participants in the "where" experiment show a sensitivity to playback speed even when taking temporal differences into account, closest to either the Reference-Frame or Null models.

Cutting across the experiments, participant behavior is best explained as their mental simulation being sensitive to changes in frame-rate, but not fully correcting for this in the resulting properties of the content of imagined scenes.
Beyond the qualitative matches, we also compared how well the different models captured participants' sensitivity to changes in playback speed.

Both the Full and Reference-Frame-Only model's slope estimations overlap with that of people (Participants: slope = -0.71, CI = [-0.75, -0.67]; Full: slope = -0.76, CI = [-0.80, -0.71] and RF-Only: slope = -0.76, CI = [-0.80, -0.71]).
However, the Null and Content-Speed-Only models did not capture the slope of participants (Null: slope = 0.0056, CI = [-0.033, 0.045] and CS-only: slope = 0.0056, CI = [-0.033, 0.045]).
We conducted additional Mean Squared Error (MSE) and Pearson-r (r) analyses to test how each model fits participant responses.

Though MSE did not significantly differ among the models (Full: MSE = 0.26, CI = [0.09, 0.57]; RF-Only: MSE = 0.26, CI = [0.09, 0.57]; Null: MSE = 0.50, CI = [0.28, 0.87]; Content-Speed-Only: MSE = 0.50, CI = [0.28, 0.87]), Pearson-r reveals that Full and RF-Only best capture the human falling time estimation.
The confidence intervals are obtained by bootstrapping participants.

Study 2.
Participants saw videos of a real scene, in which a person rolled a green yoga ball off the edge of a balcony.
Participants were asked to continue the motion of the ball in their mind, and either answer when it hit the ground (Experiment 2a, top) or where it landed (Experiment 2b, bottom).

As in Experiment 1a, participants in the "when" experiment showed a sensitivity to changes in playback speed, in line with models that adjust for frame-rate in mental simulation, and not in line with those that do not.
Furthermore, and unlike Experiment 1b, participants in the "where" experiment were able to adjust for this change in playback speed, in line with models that adjust for content velocity.

Cutting across the experiments and models, participant behavior suggests their mental simulation is sensitive to changes in frame-rate, in a way that can adjust the content speed when considering realistic scenes.
